NICE CKS Round-Up — August 2026: Recent Updates for UK Primary Care

18 September 2026 4 min read By Dr Tim Hamilton, Consultant in Palliative Medicine, NHS Wales

Six topics were updated in August 2026, and every one of them was a scheduled review rather than a rewrite. None carried major changes to clinical recommendations.

That is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up. But three of the six gained something genuinely useful, and one of those is a rename that will break a bookmark.

The updates that matter this month

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome. Reviewed against an April 2026 literature search, with no major changes to clinical recommendations. Within that: follow-up recommendations in primary care were amended to reflect pragmatic clinical practice, CTS-6 is recommended to support diagnostic decisions, and referral for nerve conduction studies should be reserved for atypical cases and diagnostic uncertainty. The information on the Tinel sign was updated to reflect a recent systematic review. Takeaway: the most practically useful item this month. It puts a validated clinical score at the front of the pathway and is explicit that electrodiagnostic testing is for uncertainty, not confirmation of the obvious — worth reading in full if you refer for nerve conduction studies routinely.
  • Palliative care — breathlessness. Renamed from "Palliative care — dyspnoea", in line with other CKS topics. The topic was restructured, including consolidation of the assessment section into a single node, and the recommendations were updated in line with current evidence. Web links to patient and carer information were added. Takeaway: note that this is more than a rename — the recommendations moved as well, so re-read it rather than assuming only the title changed. A bookmark to the old name will not find it. Our palliative care digest covers the wider evidence picture in this specialty.
  • Otitis media with effusion. Reviewed against a June 2026 literature search, with no major changes to recommendations — but a new section on signs of hearing loss in infants and children has been added. Takeaway: the addition is the point. Hearing loss in a pre-verbal child is the thing that gets missed, and a prompt list of signs is exactly what a ten-minute appointment needs.
  • Faecal incontinence in adults. Reviewed against a June 2026 literature search. Minor changes to recommendations, in line with guidance from United European Gastroenterology, the European Society of Coloproctology, the European Society of Neurogastroenterology and Motility, and the European Society for Primary Care Gastroenterology. No major changes. Takeaway: no change to the overall approach; the topic has been brought into line with current European specialist guidance.
  • Contraception — barrier methods and spermicides. Reviewed against a July 2026 literature search, with no changes to clinical recommendations. The topic is confirmed as in line with the WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th edition, 2025. Takeaway: no practice change — but note the alignment is to WHO MEC, which is a different document from the UKMEC that the contraception assessment topic was aligned to in July.
  • Pre-patellar bursitis. Reviewed against a July 2026 literature search. No major changes to the recommendations. Takeaway: no practice change; the topic has been confirmed as current.

How to use this

Two things are worth your time this month: the carpal tunnel diagnostic pathway if you see hand symptoms regularly, and the palliative care breathlessness topic if you work in that space — because its recommendations changed alongside the rename, which is easy to miss when a title change is the headline.

Everything else is awareness. A review that changes nothing still tells you something: the topic has been checked against a recent literature search and confirmed as current. NICE fully reviews every CKS topic on a five-year cycle, and sooner when significant new evidence appears, so a quiet month is the system working rather than the system idling.

A note on what this post is — and is not

This is a summary for awareness. It is not a substitute for the NICE CKS topic pages, which are the authoritative and current source. Always confirm the recommendation on the CKS topic page before acting on it — that matters most for the carpal tunnel and palliative care breathlessness changes above. Clinical decisions remain the responsibility of the treating clinician.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is NICE CKS?

NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS) are concise, regularly updated summaries of the evidence base and best-practice guidance for over 370 primary-care topics, free to access in the UK. Topics are fully reviewed every five years, and sooner if significant new evidence emerges. NICE produces up to 10 new topics and more than 65 updates each year.

Which CKS topics were updated in August 2026?

Six, and all six were scheduled reviews rather than rewrites: carpal tunnel syndrome, contraception (barrier methods and spermicides), faecal incontinence in adults, otitis media with effusion, palliative care breathlessness, and pre-patellar bursitis. None carried major changes to clinical recommendations, but three gained additions worth knowing about.

What changed in the CKS carpal tunnel syndrome topic?

No major changes to clinical recommendations. The recommendations on follow-up in primary care were amended to reflect pragmatic clinical practice, CTS-6 is recommended to support diagnostic decisions, and referral for nerve conduction studies should be reserved for atypical cases and diagnostic uncertainty. The information on the Tinel sign was updated to reflect a recent systematic review. Confirm the current recommendation on the CKS topic page before changing how you investigate an individual patient.

Why was palliative care dyspnoea renamed?

The topic is now called palliative care breathlessness, changed in line with other CKS topics. It also underwent minor restructuring, including consolidation of the assessment section into a single node, and the recommendations were updated in line with current evidence. Web links to patient and carer information were added. So this is not only a rename — the recommendations moved too.

Where can I see the full list of recent CKS changes?

The authoritative source is the NICE CKS website, which lists new and updated topics with dates and a short description of what changed in each. This post is a summary for awareness — always confirm the current recommendation against the CKS topic page before acting on it.
